175

 

(b) Forms and payment of fees. The planning director shall provide applicants with forms, designating therein the amount of fees to be paid. All fees shall be payable to the city finance department.

(c) Refund of fees.

(1) Incomplete applications. If an applicant fails to provide a complete application and the application is withdrawn by the applicant or is deemed withdrawn and returned pursuant to section 599.300(c), the city shall retain the first one hundred dollars ($100.00) of the total fees paid for the project. Any sum paid over the amount to be retained shall be refunded.

(2) Complete applications. If an applicant withdraws a complete application before the scheduled public hearing, or in the case of an application for administrative review, before the application is decided by the planning director or zoning administrator, the city shall retain the first one hundred dollars ($100.00) of the total fees paid for the project, or such proportion of the fee paid as determined by the costs to the city to process the application up to the time it was withdrawn compared to the costs to completely process the application, whichever is greater. Any sum paid over the amount to be retained shall be refunded. If the scheduled public hearing is held, or if the application is decided by the planning director or zoning administrator, no fees shall be refunded, whether or not the application is withdrawn, approved or denied.

(3) Exception. The city shall refund the total amount of the fees paid for any application that was accepted by the planning director or zoning administrator in error.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Appeals of decisions of the planning director
children.text:
All findings and decisions of the planning director, building official, or other official involved in the administration or the enforcement of these heritage preservation regulations shall be final subject to appeal to the heritage preservation commission, except that an appeal involving a violation of Title 5 of the Minneapolis Code of Ordinances, Building Code, or Title 12 of the Minneapolis Code of Ordinances, Housing, shall be as provided in the written order. Appeals may be initiated by any affected person by filing the appeal with the planning director on a form approved by the planning director and shall be accompanied by all required supporting information, as specified in section 599.300, and fees as specified in section 599.320. All appeals shall be filed within ten (10) calendar days of the date of the decision. Timely filing of an appeal shall stay all proceedings in the action appealed. No action shall be taken by any person to alter the property in any manner until after a final decision has been made by the heritage preservation commission, unless the planning director certifies to the commission, with service of a copy to the applicant, that a stay would cause imminent peril to life or property, in which case the proceedings shall not be stayed. The commission shall hold a public hearing on each complete application for an appeal as provided in section 599.310. All findings and decisions of the commission concerning appeals shall be final, subject to appeal to the city council as specified in section 599.410.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Appeals of decisions of the heritage preservation commission
children.text:
All decisions of the heritage preservation commission shall be final subject to appeal to the city council and the right of subsequent judicial review. Appeals may be initiated by any affected person by filing the appeal with the planning director on a form approved by the planning director and shall be accompanied by all required supporting information, as specified in section 599.300, and fees as specified in section 599.320. All appeals shall be filed within ten (10) calendar days of the date of the decision by the commission. No action shall be taken by any person to alter the property in any manner until expiration of the ten-day appeal period and, if an appeal is filed pursuant to this section, until after a final decision has been made by the city council. Not less than ten (10) days before the public hearing to be held by the city council to consider the appeal, the planning director shall mail notice of the hearing to the property owner and the surrounding property owners who were sent notice of the public hearing before the commission. The failure to give mailed notice to individual property owners or defects in the notice shall not invalidate the proceedings, provided a bona fide attempt to comply with this section has been made.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Purpose
children.text:
This article is established to promote the orderly identification of potential historic resources, to make determinations of local eligibility accessible to interested parties, and to support the historic designation process.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Identification of potential historic resources
children.text:
Potential historic resources shall include both potential historic landmarks and potential historic districts, as defined in this chapter. Potential historic resources may be identified by the planning director through the analysis of applications for determinations of local eligibility, wrecking permits, and through historic reconnaissance surveys and other studies conducted by or on behalf of the planning director. The planning director shall maintain a roster of potential historic resources which have been formally identified, along with related records of the determinations, reviews, surveys and/or studies which lead to their identification.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Determination of local eligibility
children.text:
(a) Purpose. Determinations of local eligibility are established to provide for the preliminary analysis of the historic significance and integrity of a property or collection of properties for the purpose of determining whether the property or collection of properties are eligible for local historic designation.

(b) Procedure and decision-making body. An application for a determination of local eligibility may be submitted by any interested party on an application form approved by the planning director and shall be accompanied by all required supporting information as determined by the planning director. The planning director shall make decisions on applications for determinations of local eligibility, subject to appeal to the heritage preservation commission as specified in section 599.400.

(1) Potential historic district determination of local eligibility. In the case of an application for a determination of local eligibility for a potential historic district, required supporting information shall include:

a. A historic resource survey encompassing the full extent of the potential historic district;

b. A defined boundary for the potential historic district;

c. A written statement addressing the relationship of the potential historic district to the criteria of significance for local historic designation; and

d. Whether the potential historic district maintains historic integrity.

(c) Required findings or criteria. The planning director shall determine that a property or collection of properties are eligible for local designation and constitutes a potential historic resource upon finding both of the following:

(1) The property or collection of properties is believed to meet at least one (1) of the criteria of significance for local designation as a landmark or historic district contained in section 599.710.

(2) The property or collection of properties maintains historic integrity.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Purpose
children.text:
This article is established to consider the preservation of potential historic resources by describing the process for proposing and recommending the designation of landmarks and historic districts.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Permitted nominators
children.text:
A nomination for designation as a landmark or historic district may be submitted pursuant to this article by any of the following:

(1) A member of the heritage preservation commission.

(2) A member of the city council.

(3) The mayor.

(4) The planning director.

(5) In the case of a nomination for designation as a landmark, any person with a legal or equitable interest in the subject property.

(6) In the case of a nomination for designation as a historic district, any person with a legal or equitable interest in one (1) of the subject properties, having first obtained the consent of the owners of a simple majority of the properties which constitute the proposed historic district.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Potential historic resource requirement
children.text:
Only properties which have been previously determined to be potential historic resources pursuant to Article V, Potential Historic Resources, may be nominated for historic designation. Nominations for historic designation submitted for properties which have not been previously determined to be potential historic resources shall be invalid. Nominations submitted by a member of the city council or the mayor shall be exempt from this requirement.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Application for nomination
children.text:
(a) Nomination application. Nomination of a property to be considered for designation as a landmark or historic district shall be submitted to the planning director on a nomination application form approved by the planning director and shall be accompanied by all required supporting information as determined by the planning director.

(b) Procedure and decision-making body. The heritage preservation commission shall hold a public hearing as provided in section 599.310 and make decisions on nominations for historic designations, subject to appeal to the city council as specified in section 599.410.

(c) Required findings or criteria. The heritage preservation commission may approve or deny the nomination for historic designation upon making each of the following findings:

(1) The information provided is sufficient to recommend a designation study.

(2) The property or collection of properties meets at least one (1) local criterion contained in section 599.710 to be studied as a historic landmark or district.

(3) The property or collection of properties retains sufficient historic integrity to be studied as a historic landmark or district.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Designation study
children.text:
(a) Preparation of study. For each nomination for historic designation approved by the heritage preservation commission, the planning director shall prepare or cause to be prepared a designation study for the property. In cases where an application for demolition initiated by a property owner results in an approved nomination for historic designation, the planning director may determine that the property owner bears the full financial responsibility of conducting the designation study. In all cases, the planning director shall define the scope of services for a designation study, review qualifications of agents conducting the study, and make a determination of what constitutes a final submission upon completion.

(b) Study requirements. Complete designation studies shall include the following, at minimum:

(1) The following information and documentation for each individual property included in the proposed landmark or historic district designation:

a. The address;

b. The property identification number;

c. A physical description;

d. The date of construction; and

e. Photos.

(2) For proposed historic districts, an additional physical description of the district as a whole.

(3) A narrative discussion of the historic background of the proposed landmark or historic district.

(4) An explanation of how the proposed landmark or historic district meets or does not meet each of the significance criteria for local designation contained in section 599.710.

(5) An explanation of how the proposed landmark or historic district does or does not retain historic integrity under each of the seven (7) aspects of integrity.

(6) Proposed boundaries of the landmark or historic district.

(7) A proposed period of significance.

(8) A list of proposed contributing and non-contributing resources.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Interim protection
children.text:
(a) Purpose. Interim protection is established to protect a property or collection of properties from demolition or alterations that may destroy or negatively affect the character-defining features of such property or collection of properties during the designation study process.

(b) Effective date. Interim protection shall be in effect from the date of the heritage preservation commission's decision to commence a designation study of a property or collection of properties until the city council makes a decision regarding the designation, or for sixteen (16) months, whichever comes first. Interim protection may not be extended.

(c) Scope of restrictions. While under interim protection, the following restrictions shall apply:

(1) Proposed landmarks. During the interim protection period for proposed landmarks, no alteration of a property shall be allowed except where authorized by a preservation permit, administrative preservation application or a commission preservation application. No demolition of a property shall be allowed for a proposed landmark under interim protection except where authorized by an application for demolition of designated property.

(2) Proposed historic districts. During the interim protection period for proposed historic districts, no demolition of a property shall be allowed except where authorized by an application for demolition of designated property.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Purpose
children.text:
This article is established to promote the preservation of potential historic resources by providing for the review, consideration, and designation of landmarks and historic districts.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Significance criteria
children.text:
The following criteria shall be considered in determining whether a property is worthy of designation as a landmark or historic district because of its historical, cultural, architectural, archaeological, or engineering significance:

(1) The property is associated with significant events or with periods that exemplify broad patterns of cultural, political, economic, or social history.

(2) The property is associated with the lives of significant persons or groups.

(3) The property contains or is associated with distinctive elements of city or neighborhood identity.

(4) The property embodies the distinctive characteristics of an architectural or engineering type or style, or method of construction.

(5) The property exemplifies a landscape design or development pattern distinguished by innovation, rarity, uniqueness, or quality of design or detail.

(6) The property exemplifies works of master builders, engineers, designers, artists, craftsmen, or architects.

(7) The property has yielded, or may be likely to yield, information important in prehistory or history.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Historic integrity
State Historic Preservation Office review
children.text:
The planning director shall submit all proposed designations to the State Historic Preservation Office for review and comment. The State Historic Preservation Office shall have sixty (60) days from said date of submittal to provide comments to the planning director.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Designation procedure and decision
children.text:
(a) Procedure and decision-making body. The heritage preservation commission shall hold a public hearing as provided in section 599.310 and make a recommendation to the city council on all designations. The city council shall make decisions on all designations.

(b) Required findings or criteria. After considering the designation criteria contained in section 599.710, the information contained in the designation study, the State Historic Preservation Office's comments, the planning director's report, and all public testimony and evidence received at the public hearing related to the designation, the heritage preservation commission and city council shall make the following findings:

(1) The property or collection of properties meets at least one (1) local criterion to be designated as a landmark or historic district.

(2) The property or collection of properties retains sufficient historic integrity to be designated as a landmark or historic district.

(c) Designation decision. The city council shall have one hundred eighty (180) days to take final action on the designation following the heritage preservation commission's recommendation. In the absence of a decision within one hundred eighty (180) days, or should the city council deny a designation, a new nomination for the same designation may not be submitted for a period of three (3) years from the end of the one hundred eighty (180) days.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Designation amendments
children.text:
(a) Amendments to designations. Amendments to designations may be considered as provided in this section.

(b) Amendment to the period of significance and criteria of significance of a landmark or historic district. The planning director may determine the criteria of significance and period of significance for a landmark or historic district, based on necessary research and evaluation, when such information is not included in designations existing on the effective date of this ordinance. For landmarks and historic districts with designations that include a period of significance and criteria of significance, amendments shall be submitted and considered as a nomination for historic designation, according to the procedures set forth in Article VI of this chapter.

(c) Amendment to the contributing or non-contributing status of a landmark or property in a historic district. The planning director may determine whether resources or properties are contributing or non-contributing to landmarks or historic districts when such information is not included in a designation existing on the effective date of this ordinance. Amendments to the contributing or non-contributing status of designated resources may be completed by the planning director with necessary research and evaluation.

(d) Amendment to boundaries of a landmark or historic district. The boundaries of a landmark or historic district may be expanded through an amendment, but not reduced. Amendments to expand the boundaries of a landmark or historic district shall be submitted and considered as a nomination for historic designation, according to the procedures set forth in Article VI of this chapter.

(e) Removing a landmark from designation. The planning director may propose the removal of a landmark from designation if such landmark has been destroyed by fire or other peril. For each landmark proposed for removal from designation, the planning director shall prepare a report including all relevant supporting materials and make a recommendation to the heritage preservation commission. The heritage preservation commission shall hold a public hearing pursuant to section 599.310 regarding the removal and make a recommendation to the city council. The city council shall consider the heritage preservation commission's recommendation and take final action.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Purpose
children.text:
This article is established to promote the protection of landmarks and historic districts by providing for the adoption of historic design guidelines to guide the review of alterations to designated properties. Historic design guidelines protect the historic character of designated properties based on conditions and context specific to a landmark or historic district by providing guidance for their preservation, rehabilitation, and development.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Historic design guidelines
children.text:
(a) In general. The planning director may propose the adoption of historic design guidelines specific to individual landmarks and historic districts for consideration by the heritage preservation commission and city council. The adoption of historic design guidelines is optional. They shall follow and not append a designation by the heritage preservation commission and city council. Historic design guidelines shall be utilized in the review of alterations proposed for designated landmarks and historic districts as provided in Article X of this chapter.

(b) The Secretary of the Interior's Standards. Historic design guidelines will follow the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation. In the absence of historic design guidelines, the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation will be used to review alterations to designated properties.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: State Historic Preservation Office review
children.text:
The planning director shall submit all proposed historic design guidelines to the State Historic Preservation Office for review and comment. The State Historic Preservation Office shall have sixty (60) days from said date of submittal to provide comments to the planning director.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Consideration and adoption
children.text:
(a) Procedure and decision-making body. The planning director shall present all proposed historic design guidelines to the heritage preservation commission and city council for consideration and adoption. The heritage preservation commission shall hold a public hearing as provided in section 599.310 and make recommendations to the city council on all proposed historic design guidelines. The city council shall make the final decision on the adoption of all historic design guidelines.

(b) Required findings or criteria. The heritage preservation commission and city council may adopt historic design guidelines upon making the following findings:

(1) The historic design guidelines meet the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation.

(2) The historic design guidelines preserve the historic character of the landmark or historic district.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Purpose
children.text:
This article is established to protect potential historic resources and designated properties from demolition by describing the processes used by the planning director and the heritage preservation commission to review and intervene in all proposed building demolitions.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Review of demolitions
children.text:
(a) In general. All demolitions of principal buildings or structures shall be reviewed pursuant to this chapter prior to a wrecking permit being granted. Nothing in this article shall prevent the building official from authorizing an emergency demolition to correct dangerous or unsafe conditions pursuant to section 599.50(b).

(b) All wrecking permits. The planning director shall review all submitted building, wrecking or demolition permit applications which constitute the demolition of a principal building or structure to determine whether the subject property has been designated as a landmark or part of a historic district, identified as a potential historic resource or may constitute a potential historic resource. If the property is not a designated landmark or part of a historic district and is determined by the planning director to not be a potential historic resource, approval of the building, wrecking or demolition permit shall be granted.

(c) Potential historic resources. A building, wrecking or demolition permit authorizing the demolition of a potential historic resource shall not be granted without an application for demolition of potential historic resource having been first approved.

(d) Designated properties. A building, wrecking or demolition permit authorizing the demolition of a property designated as a historic landmark or part of a historic district shall not be granted without an application for demolition of designated property having been first approved.

(e) Property under interim protection. A building, wrecking or demolition permit authorizing the demolition of a property under interim protection shall not be granted without an application for demolition of designated property having been first approved.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Application for demolition of potential historic resource
children.text:
(a) Application generally. An application for demolition of potential historic resource shall be submitted to the planning director by any person having a legal or equitable interest in a property on an application form approved by the planning director and shall be accompanied by all required supporting information as determined by the planning director.

(b) Procedure and decision-making body. The heritage preservation commission shall hold a public hearing as provided in section 599.310 and make decisions on applications for demolition of potential historic resource, subject to appeal to the city council as specified in section 599.410.

(c) Required findings or criteria. The heritage preservation commission may approve the application for demolition of potential historic resource upon making at least one (1) of the following findings:

(1) The demolition is necessary to correct a structurally unsafe condition on the property based on a certified structural report from a licensed engineer.

(2) The property does not meet at least one (1) of the criteria of significance found in section 599.710 and does not retain historic integrity.

(3) A rehabilitation is not economically viable to put the property to a reasonable use based on a cost estimate for a qualified rehabilitation using the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation.

(d) Outcome.

(1) Upon the approval of an application for demolition of potential historic resource, the planning director shall grant all building, wrecking or demolition permits requested for the subject property.

(2) In the case of a property found to be eligible for designation as a potential historic landmark, the denial of an application for demolition of potential historic resource shall constitute the approval of its nomination for historic designation. The subject property shall be placed under interim protection and the planning director shall prepare or cause to be prepared a designation study pursuant to Article VI, Nomination for Historic Designation, and Article VII, Historic Designation.

(3) In the case of a property believed by the planning director to retain sufficient historic integrity to communicate its significance as part of a potential historic district but found to be not eligible for designation as a potential historic landmark, the denial of an application for demolition of potential historic resource shall result in a demolition delay. For a period of ninety (90) days following the denial, the planning director shall not grant any building, wrecking or demolition permits which constitute the demolition of the principal building or structure on the property. During the period of demolition delay, permitted nominators may bring forth a nomination for designation of the potential historic district pursuant to Article VI, Nomination for Historic Designation. If at the end of the period of demolition delay no complete nomination application has been received, the planning director shall grant all building, wrecking, or demolition permits requested for the subject property.

(e) Mitigation plan. The heritage preservation commission may require a mitigation plan as a condition of any approval for demolition of potential historic resource. Such plan may include the documentation of the property by measured drawings, photographic recording, historic research, interpretive materials, or other means appropriate to memorialize the significance of the property.

(f) Demolition delay. The heritage preservation commission may stay the release of any building, wrecking or demolition permit which constitute the demolition of the principal building or structure on the property for up to ninety (90) days as a condition of approval for a demolition of potential historic resource to allow parties interested in preserving the potential historic resource a reasonable opportunity to act to protect it. The authority to require a demolition delay as a condition of approval for an application for demolition of potential historic resource pursuant to this section is distinct in purpose and operation from the demolition delay inherent to the denial of an application for demolition of potential historic resource pursuant to section 599.920(d)(3).

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Application for demolition of designated property
children.text:
(a) Application generally. An application for demolition of designated property shall be submitted to the planning director by any person having a legal or equitable interest in a property on an application form approved by the planning director and shall be accompanied by all required supporting information as determined by the planning director.

(b) Procedure and decision-making body. The heritage preservation commission shall hold a public hearing as provided in section 599.310 and make decisions on applications for demolition of designated property, subject to appeal to the city council as specified in section 599.410.

(c) Required findings or criteria. The heritage preservation commission may approve the application for demolition of designated property upon making one (1) of the following findings:

(1) The demolition is necessary to correct a structurally unsafe condition on the property based on a certified structural report from a licensed engineer.

(2) Due to a loss of historic integrity and limited economic value of the existing building or structure, reasonable alternatives to demolition do not exist. In order to determine that reasonable alternatives to demolition do not exist, each of the following conditions must be met, if applicable:

a. The property does not retain historic integrity.

b. In the case of a property which is part of a designated historic district, the property is not believed to meet at least one (1) of the significance criteria as a potential historic landmark and retain historic integrity as such, nor is the property believed to retain sufficient integrity to communicate the significance of a potential historic district outside of the property's existing designation.

c. In the case of a property which is a designated historic landmark or a contributing resource to a historic district, a rehabilitation is not economically viable to put the property to a reasonable use based on a cost estimate for a qualified rehabilitation using the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation.

(d) Outcome.

(1) Upon the approval of an application for demolition of designated property, the planning director shall grant all building, wrecking or demolition permits requested for the subject property.

(2) In the case of a property which is part of a designated historic district and is found to be eligible for designation as a potential historic landmark, the denial of an application for demolition of designated property shall constitute the approval of its nomination for historic designation. The subject property shall be placed under interim protection and the planning director shall prepare or cause to be prepared a designation study pursuant to Article VI, Nomination for Historic Designation, and Article VII, Historic Designation.

(3) In the case of a property which is part of a designated historic district and is believed to retain sufficient historic integrity to communicate its significance as part of a potential historic district outside of its existing designation but found to be not eligible for designation as a potential historic landmark, the denial of an application for demolition of designated property shall result in a demolition delay. For a period of ninety (90) days following the denial, the planning director shall not grant any building, wrecking, or demolition permits which constitute the demolition of the principal building or structure on the property. During the period of demolition delay, permitted nominators may bring forth a nomination for designation of the potential historic district pursuant to Article VI, Nomination for Historic Designation. If at the end of the period of demolition delay no complete nomination application has been received, the planning director shall grant all building, wrecking, or demolition permits requested for demolition of the subject property.

(e) Mitigation plan. The heritage preservation commission may require a mitigation plan as a condition of any approval for demolition of designated property. Such plan may include the documentation of the property by measured drawings, photographic recording, historic research, interpretive materials, or other means appropriate to memorialize the significance of the property.

(f) Demolition delay. The heritage preservation commission may stay the release of any building, wrecking or demolition permit which constitute the demolition of the principal building or structure on the property for up to ninety (90) days as a condition of approval for a demolition of designated property to allow parties interested in preserving the historic resource a reasonable opportunity to act to protect it. The authority to require a demolition delay as a condition of approval for an application for demolition of potential historic resource pursuant to this section is distinct in purpose and operation from the demolition delay inherent to the denial of an application for demolition of designated property pursuant to section 599.930(d)(3).

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Description
children.text:
This article is established to protect landmarks, historic districts, and potential historic landmarks under interim protection, by providing the planning director and heritage preservation commission with authority to review and approve or deny all proposed alterations to a landmark, property in a historic district, or potential historic landmark under interim protection.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Historic design review required
children.text:
All alterations to designated landmarks, properties which are part of a designated historic district and potential historic landmarks under interim protection shall be reviewed pursuant to this chapter.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Administrative preservation reviews, generally
children.text:
(a) Purpose. Certain preservation decisions may be made, and preservation permits issued, following a review that does not involve a formal application form or process. However, based on the degree of complexity or city staff time involved in the review of certain uses, buildings, or structures, the planning director may develop administrative review processes and applications that lead to decisions about compliance with the heritage preservation ordinance and comprehensive plan. The heritage preservation ordinance does not list every such scope of work which may require an administrative application. Forms for preservation applications are provided by the planning director. Where a fee is charged, such fee is listed in Table 599-1, Fees.

(b) Procedures and decision-makers. Following submittal of information required by this ordinance and any applicable application forms, the planning director shall make decisions on administrative reviews and applications, subject to appeal to the heritage preservation commission as specified in section 599.400.

(c) Required findings or criteria. Unless specific findings or criteria are listed elsewhere in the heritage preservation ordinance or in the application form provided by the planning director, administrative reviews include a review for compliance with the applicable provisions of the heritage preservation ordinance and any applicable design guidelines or recommendations within the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Preservation permit
children.text:
(a) Purpose. A preservation permit shall be obtained from the planning director prior to any of the following:

(1) The construction, addition, relocation, demolition in whole or in part, and installation of features, systems, or material changes, including signs and awnings, affecting the exterior of a landmark, property in a historic district or property under interim protection, or the designated or nominated interior of any building or structure.

(2) Any site work that affects the character-defining features of a designated landscape, landscape associated with a designated property or property under interim protection or identified archaeological resource.

(b) Procedure and decision-making body. An application for a preservation permit shall include a plan dimensioned or annotated as to accurately show the proposed building, structure, or alteration as well as any materials specifications, photos, or other information required by the planning director to determine heritage preservation compliance. The planning director shall make decisions on preservation permits and shall affix their stamp on approved plans. Such stamp shall serve as the preservation permit. Where a building permit has been reviewed and approved by the planning director for the purpose of compliance with this heritage preservation ordinance, such approval shall serve as the preservation permit.

(c) Required findings or criteria. The permit includes a review for consistency with the regulations of this heritage preservation ordinance and any applicable design guidelines or recommendations within the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation. In such instances where the permit requires additional land use review by the planning director, board of adjustment, city planning commission, heritage preservation commission, or city council, the planning director shall not grant the preservation permit until the applicable review body grants approval, the appeal period has expired, and such plans are consistent with the approval granted by the applicable decision-making body.

(d) Revocability of preservation permit. Any permit, document, or approval issued by the planning director may be revoked upon a violation of this heritage preservation ordinance or any conditions under which it is issued, subject to the provisions of Article XIV, Enforcement.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Administrative preservation application
children.text:
(a) Purpose. Administrative preservation applications are administrative applications established to evaluate compliance with applicable historic design guidelines and the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation for alterations that affect historic materials and will have a visual impact on designated properties or properties under interim protection. This application may review partial demolitions of non-historic buildings or structures and substantial rehabilitation projects that have an approved part 2 historic rehabilitation tax credit application by the State Historic Preservation Office and the National Park Service.

(b) Procedure and decision-making body. An administrative preservation application shall be filed by any person having a legal or equitable interest in a property on a form approved by the planning director and shall be accompanied by all required supporting information as determined by the planning director. The planning director shall make decisions on administrative preservation applications, subject to appeal to the heritage preservation commission as specified in section 599.400.

(c) Required findings or criteria. The planning director shall approve the administrative preservation application upon making each of the following findings:

(1) The alteration is consistent with the applicable design guidelines.

(2) The alteration is consistent with the applicable recommendations within the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation.

(3) The alteration is consistent with the spirit and intent of the preservation ordinance and the applicable policies of the comprehensive plan.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Commission preservation application
children.text:
(a) Purpose. Commission preservation applications are public hearing applications established to evaluate compliance with applicable historic design guidelines and the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation for new construction of primary or accessory buildings, substantial rehabilitation projects, and demolition of historic accessory buildings or structures on designated properties or properties under interim protection. This application shall also be used for alterations that do not meet applicable historic design guidelines and the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation, alterations that will result in extensive replacement of historic materials, and alterations that will have a major visual impact.

(b) Procedure and decision-making body. A commission preservation application shall be filed by any person having a legal or equitable interest in a property on a form approved by the planning director and shall be accompanied by all required supporting information as determined by the planning director. The heritage preservation commission shall hold a public hearing as provided in section 599.310 and make decisions on commission preservation applications, subject to appeal to the city council as specified in section 599.410.

(c) Required findings or criteria. The heritage preservation commission shall approve the commission preservation application upon making each of the following findings:

(1) The alteration is consistent with the applicable design guidelines.

(2) The alteration is consistent with the applicable recommendations within the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation.

(3) The alteration is consistent with the spirit and intent of the preservation ordinance and the applicable policies of the comprehensive plan.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Changes in approved plan
children.text:
(a) Minor changes to administrative preservation application approvals. Minor changes to an approved administrative preservation application may be authorized by the planning director where it is determined by the planning director that the minor changes are consistent with the applicable historic design guidelines or the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation.

(b) Minor changes to commission preservation application approvals. Minor changes to an approved commission preservation application may be authorized by the planning director where it is determined by the planning director that the changes are unsubstantial and are consistent with the approval made by the heritage preservation commission.

(c) Other changes. Changes to an approved commission preservation application other than changes determined by the planning director to be minor shall require an amendment to the approval by the heritage preservation commission. The requirements for application and approval of commission preservation application amendments shall be the same as the requirements for original approval.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Purpose
children.text:
This article is established to encourage the preservation and reuse of landmarks and properties in historic districts by providing a process to consider the departure from the literal requirements of any of the applicable zoning regulations.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Application for historic exception
children.text:
(a) Application generally. An application for historic exception shall be filed by any person having a legal or equitable interest in a property on a form approved by the planning director and shall be accompanied by all required supporting information as determined by the planning director.

(b) Procedure and decision-making body. The heritage preservation commission shall hold a public hearing as provided in section 599.310 and make decisions on applications for historic exception, subject to appeal to the city council as specified in section 599.410.

(c) Required findings or criteria. The heritage preservation commission may approve the application for a historic exception upon making each of the following findings:

(1) The exception is compatible with the preservation of the designated property and with other properties in the area.

(2) The exception is necessary to alleviate practical difficulties due to special conditions or circumstances unique to the designated property and not created by the applicant.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Changes in approved historic exception
children.text:
Changes to an approved historic exception shall require a new historic exception application. The requirements for application and approval of a change to a historic exception shall be the same as the requirements for original approval.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.heading: ARTICLE XII.
children.title: NATIONAL REGISTER OF HISTORIC PLACES NOMINATION
Purpose
children.text:
This article is established to support the preservation programs of the National Park Service, the State Historic Preservation Office, and the city to promote alignment between these programs and the work of the heritage preservation commission by describing the process to comment on a nomination to the National Register of Historic Places.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: National Register nomination
children.text:
Upon notification by the State Historic Preservation Office that a property in the city has been nominated for listing in the National Register of Historic Places, the planning director shall review the nomination and bring the nomination forth for review and comment by the heritage preservation commission.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Public meeting and comment
children.text:
(a) In general. The heritage preservation commission shall review and comment on a National Register nomination at a public meeting. The heritage preservation commission shall not hold a public hearing pursuant to section 599.310 regarding a National Register nomination. Notification shall be made, and public comment shall be taken pursuant to this article.

(b) Notification procedures. Notification of a National Register nomination shall be given pursuant to this section. The failure to give mailed notice to affected property owners, or defects in the notice, shall not invalidate the proceedings, provided that a bona fide attempt to comply with this section has been made.

(1) Newspaper of general circulation. The planning director shall publish notice of the time, place and purpose of the public meeting at least once, not less than ten (10) calendar days before the meeting, in a newspaper of general circulation.

(2) Affected property owner. The planning director shall mail notice to the owner of record of the subject property not less than ten (10) calendar days before the meeting.

(3) Mayor. The planning director shall transmit notice to the mayor not less than ten (10) calendar days before the meeting.

(c) Procedures. The meeting shall be open to the public. Any person may appear and provide comment at the meeting as directed by the chair or acting chair. The commission shall make and consider motions about the nomination and its relationship to the criteria for listing in the National Register of Historic Places and to direct the planning director to submit its comments to the State Historic Preservation Office accompanied by any other comments deemed appropriate by the commission.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Purpose
children.text:
This article is established to ensure that landmarks, historic districts, and properties under interim protection are properly maintained and protected against deterioration.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Duty to maintain
children.text:
All landmarks, historic districts, and properties under interim protection shall be kept in a state of maintenance and repair as required under Title 5 of the Minneapolis Code of Ordinances, Building Code, and Title 12 of the Minneapolis Code of Ordinances, Housing, and with all other applicable regulations. All designated properties or properties under interim protection shall also be maintained as a secured building or structure and weathertight.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Prevention of deterioration
children.text:
No person with a legal or equitable interest in a landmark, property in a historic district or property under interim protection, whether occupied or not, shall permit the property to fall into a serious state of disrepair or to remain in a serious state of disrepair so as to materially impair the historic integrity of the landmark, property in a historic district, or property under interim protection.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Purpose
children.text:
This article is established to ensure that the requirements of this chapter are enforced in accordance with the procedures set forth herein.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Complaints regarding violations
children.text:
The planning director and building official shall have the authority to investigate any complaint alleging a violation of this chapter or the conditions of approval granted pursuant to this chapter and to take such action as is warranted in accordance with the procedures set forth in this chapter.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Procedure upon discovery of violations
children.text:
(a) Notice of violation. The city shall provide a written notice to the property owner or to any person responsible for such violation, identifying the property in question, indicating the nature of the violation, and ordering the action necessary to correct it, including a reasonable time period to remedy the violation. The written notice shall advise that the decision or order may be appealed to the heritage preservation commission in accordance with the provisions of section 599.400. Additional written notices may be provided at the discretion of the enforcement official. Where the violation involves work being done contrary to the provisions of this chapter, the city may order the work stopped. No further work shall be undertaken while a stop-work order is in effect.

(b) Enforcement without notice. Whenever the city finds that an emergency exists in relation to the enforcement of the provisions of this chapter which requires immediate action to protect the health, safety or welfare of occupants of any building, structure or the public, they may seek immediate enforcement without prior written notice, notwithstanding any other provision of this chapter.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Fees for reinspection of property to determine abatement
children.text:
(a) Initial inspection and first reinspection. There shall be no fee charged for an initial inspection to determine the existence of a heritage preservation ordinance violation, nor any fee for the first reinspection to determine compliance with an order to correct a heritage preservation ordinance violation.

(b) Subsequent reinspection. A two-hundred-dollar ($200.00) fee shall be charged for each subsequent reinspection occurring after the due date for compliance with an order.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Penalties and remedies for violations
children.text:
Violations of the provisions of this heritage preservation ordinance or the conditions of any preservation approval granted thereunder may be enforced by any one (1), all, or any combination of the following penalties and remedies:

(1) Violations shall be punishable as criminal offenses as stated in section 1.30 of the Minneapolis Code of Ordinances.

(2) Violations may be enforced as administrative offenses pursuant to Chapter 2 of the Minneapolis Code of Ordinances.

(3) This heritage preservation ordinance may also be enforced by injunction, abatement, mandamus, or any other appropriate remedy in any court of competent jurisdiction.

(4) Each day that any violation continues after notification by the city that such violation exists shall be considered a separate offense for the purpose of the penalties and remedies specified in this section.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025)

children.title: Definitions
children.text:
Unless otherwise expressly stated, or unless the context clearly indicates a different meaning, the words and phrases in the following list of definitions shall, for the purposes of this chapter, have the meanings indicated. All words and phrases not defined shall have their common meaning.

Alteration. Any construction, addition, installation of features, demolition in whole or in part, relocation or material change, including signs and awnings, affecting the exterior of a landmark, property in a historic district or property under interim protection, or the designated or nominated interior of any building or structure. Also, any site work that affects the character-defining features of a designated landscape, landscape associated with a designated property or property under interim protection or identified archaeological resource.

Archaeology. The scientific study of people and their cultures through the analysis of artifacts, sites, and other remains.

Archaeological resource. The material remains of past human activity through prehistoric and historic sites that are buried below ground or extend above ground.

Building official. The individual designated by the department of community planning and economic development to serve as the city's building official pursuant to Minnesota Statutes, Section 326B.133.

Character-defining feature. A prominent or distinctive aspect, quality, physical feature or characteristic that contributes to the physical character and/or historic significance of a historic property. This may include the overall shape of the building, structure, or site, its materials, craftsmanship, decorative details, and/or various aspects of the site and environment that communicate a property's historic significance.

City council. The city council of the city of Minneapolis.

Contributing. A resource that was present during a landmark or historic district's period of significance and retains historic integrity to convey its significance.

Demolition. The act of moving or razing a building or structure including the removal or enclosure of sixty (60) percent or more of the building or structure.

Designated property. Any property included as part of a landmark or historic district designated by the city council.

Design guidelines. Specific design guidance that meets the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for rehabilitation and is adopted by the city council for landmarks and historic districts to be used in reviewing preservation permits, administrative preservation applications and commission preservation applications.

Designation study. A study and report prepared to document the historical, cultural, architectural, archaeological or engineering significance and historic integrity of a property or collection of properties.

Historic district. All properties within a defined area designated as a historic district by the city council because of the historical, cultural, architectural, archaeological or engineering significance of the district and ability of the district to convey historic integrity or designated as a historic district by state law.

Historic exception. Departure from the literal requirements of the zoning regulations governing a landmark or property in a historic district where strict adherence would cause practical difficulties due to special conditions or circumstances unique to a designated building, structure or site.

Historic integrity. The ability of a property to convey its historic significance through its physical characteristics and relationship to its historic context as evidenced by its location, design, setting, materials, workmanship, feeling and association.

Historic waiver. A waiver issued jointly by the planning director and the regulatory services director for requests relative to short term rental dwelling units in individual landmarks.

Interim protection. Protection of a property or properties from demolition or alterations that may destroy or negatively affect the character-defining features of such property during the designation study process following the heritage preservation commission's decision to commence a designation study.

Landmark. Any property, or any interior of a building, designated as a landmark by the city council because of its historical, cultural, architectural, archaeological, or engineering significance and ability to convey that significance through its historic integrity.

National Register of Historic Places. The federal government's official list of buildings, sites, districts, structures, and objects deemed worthy of preservation for their historic significance and historic integrity. It was established in 1966 as part of the National Historic Preservation Act and is overseen by the National Park Service.

Non-contributing. A resource that was built after the landmark or historic district's period of significance or does not retain historic integrity to convey its significance.

Non-historic. Features, materials, or alterations that do not date within a period of significance of a landmark or historic district.

Period of significance. The span of time during which a property or collection of properties achieved their historic significance which qualifies them for designation.

Planning director. The director of the department of community planning and economic development or their designee.

Potential historic resource. A property or collection of properties that meet the definition of a potential historic landmark or a potential historic district. An individual property may be considered a potential historic resource as part of a potential historic district if the property embodies characteristics representative of that district's significance.

Potential historic district. A contiguous or discontiguous group of two (2) or more properties that collectively are believed to meet at least one (1) of the significance criteria for local designation as a historic district and maintain historic integrity.

Potential historic landmark. A property that is believed to meet at least one (1) of the significance criteria for local designation as a landmark and maintain historic integrity.

Preservation permit. Planning director approval for any alteration where compliance with the heritage preservation ordinance, applicable historic design guidelines, and recommendations within the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation has been met.

Property. Any land, building, structure or object, surface or subsurface area, or natural or landscape feature.

Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation. The most recent standards for the treatment of historic properties under rehabilitation established by the National Park Service, United States Department of the Interior.

Secured building or structure. Any building or structure in which the roof, walls, foundation, basement, doors, windows, or other openings into the building or structure are closed by any conventional methods used in the design of buildings or are boarded up with weather resistant/weather proofed plywood (minimum acceptable grade: three-eighths inch (⅜") CD exterior) cut to fit the opening it is securing and screwed at intervals not to exceed twelve (12) inches, so as to prevent access to the building or structure from inclement weather, animals, trespassers, children, or other persons not authorized to be on the premises.

Significance. The importance of a landmark, historic district, property under interim protection, or potential historic resource, evidenced by the ability to meet at least one (1) of the seven (7) criteria of significance.

Structure. Anything constructed or erected with a more or less fixed location on the ground or in or over a body of water. A structure shall include, but not be limited to bridges, fences, walls, signs, canopies, decks, patios, antennae, piers, docks and any objects or things permanently attached to the structure. For the purposes of this chapter, a structure shall not include a building intended for human shelter.

Visual impact. The effect an alteration has on the visual appearance and surrounding environment of a building, structure, or landscape.

Weathertight. A building or structure is weathertight when it is sufficiently sealed to prevent the entry of wind, rain, or snow, allowing interior work to proceed without weather-related interruption.

Zoning administrator. The individual designated by the director of the department of community planning and economic development to serve as the city's zoning administrator or their authorized representative.

(Ord. No. 2025-053, § 1, 11-20-2025; eff. 1-1-2026)

contents.text:

children.title: Name
children.text: This charter governs a city named the "City of Minneapolis" in Hennepin County, Minnesota. For this charter's purposes, the "City" means the City of Minneapolis, and its provisions refer to the City unless the context clearly indicates otherwise.

children.title: Status
children.text: The City is a municipal corporation having adopted this home-rule charter under the Minnesota Constitution, article XII, section 4. This charter is effective as of January 1, 2015, subject to any amendment after that date.

children.title: Authority
children.text:
(a) Basic authority. Subject to applicable law, this charter and action taken under its authority are the basis for the conduct of all the City's business.

(b) Restatement and supersession. This charter fully restates and supersedes every prior version of, and any ordinance or other municipal act inconsistent with, this charter. But except as this charter or an amendment explicitly provides otherwise, the charter does not affect—

(1) any ordinance or other municipal act adopted before its adoption or its latest revision or amendment;

(2) the existence, status, function, composition, powers, or duties of any board, commission, committee, department, or other public body; or

(3) the office, tenure, powers, or duties of any officer.

(c)

Laws.

(1) Inconsistent laws superseded. This charter supersedes any special law in effect at the time of the charter's latest revision on January 1, 2015, to the extent of any inconsistency between them.

(2) Certain laws preserved. The charter does not affect any special or other law to the extent that the law—

(A) confers upon the City, or upon any board, commission, committee, department, or officer for which this charter or an ordinance provides, a power, right, duty, or role in addition to those for which the charter or ordinance provides; or

(B) covers a matter that this charter does not cover.

(d) Construction. For this charter's purposes, except as this charter otherwise provides—

(1) each term used in this charter has the same meaning as in the Minnesota constitution and statutes, and other law relating to the same subject;

(2) the canons of construction and other principles of interpretation in the Minnesota Statutes apply to this charter;

(3) each heading is a part of the charter, and may be used in interpreting its provisions, although the heading is subject to the text;

(4) the settled interpretation of any term or provision from a version of the charter before its latest revision on January 1, 2015, is valid in interpreting the revised charter to the extent that the charter carries forward the interpreted provision or term;

(5) any reference to population or other enumeration refers to the latest decennial federal census; and

(6) a "resident" means an inhabitant who resides within the City, regardless of whether he or she is a citizen within the meaning of the federal or state constitution or any other law.

children.title: Powers
children.text:
(a) Powers plenary. The City, acting through the boards, commissions, committees, departments, and officers for which this charter or an ordinance provides, may exercise any power that a municipal corporation can lawfully exercise at common law.

(1) Eminent domain. The City Council may, and any other authorized board may, establish the procedure by which the City exercises through that board its power of eminent domain, including the procedure for any appeal from an award in condemnation.

(2) Infrastructure. The City may establish, plan, build, maintain, regulate, and otherwise provide for public ways and works and any other infrastructure necessary or convenient for its residential and economic development; for the comfort, convenience, health, safety, or welfare of its residents; or for the efficient delivery of municipal services.

(b) Laws excepting home-rule cities. Whenever a law grants a power or an option to cities generally or to cities of a certain class, but excepts cities having adopted a home-rule charter, the City may nevertheless exercise the power or option if that exercise is not inconsistent with this charter, notwithstanding its having adopted this charter.

(c) Immunity. The City enjoys immunity from suit and liability for any injury resulting from—

(1) the defective condition of an ungraded street;

(2) the ground's insufficiency where a sidewalk can go but no sidewalk has been built; and

(3) any other act, omission, or condition for which a municipal corporation enjoys immunity at common law or by general or special law.

(d) Unmentioned powers. This charter's mention of certain powers does not limit the City's powers to those mentioned.

children.title: Enforcement
City
children.text: The City has the boundaries established under law.

children.title: Wards
children.text:
(a) Number. The City comprises 13 wards, designated by number. If possible, a redistricted ward keeps the number of the former ward from which its population mostly came.

(b) Characteristics. The wards must be as equal in population as practicable. Each ward must—

(1) not have a population more than five percent over or under the mean ward population, according to—

(A) the latest decennial federal census; or

(B) a special computation or enumeration ordered by the Charter Commission with respect to any particular block or tract, computed or enumerated as of the same time and in the same manner as the latest decennial federal census;

(2) consist of a compact, contiguous area, not longer than twice its width, whose boundaries lie wherever possible along the centerline of public ways and, as far as practicable, run due north-south or east-west. A lake, waterway, or other body of water within a ward does not affect these characteristics; and

(3) minimize change in existing boundaries, except as necessary in order to effect the foregoing criteria.

(c) Redistricting.

(1) Policy. The City must redistrict the wards, as this section 2.2(c) provides—

(A) after each decennial federal census;

(B) as required by general or special law or by judicial decree; or

(C) when the number of wards changes;

and may not otherwise redistrict them.

(2) Commission. For this section 2.2(c)'s purposes, the "Commission" means the Charter Commission.

(A) Advisory group. The Commission must appoint an advisory group of up to nine eligible voters in the City, who will advise the Commission about redistricting.

(i) Qualifications. Each advisory-group member must be a eligible voter in the City who has not, within the two years of being appointed—

(I) held any elected public office;

(II) appeared on a ballot listing his or her partisan affiliation in any election;

(III) worked as an employee of any political party (as defined by the Minnesota election law); or

(IV) worked as an employee for the City in any capacity other than as an election judge.

(ii) Application. Each applicant for the advisory group must submit an application to the City Clerk on a form that the Commission has approved. The Commission must accept applications for at least 45 days.

(iii) Diversity. The Commission must appoint the advisory group with due regard for diversity.

(3) Schedule. Subject to any applicable ordinance, general or special law, or judicial decree:

(A) Plan. The Commission must adopt a ward-boundary plan, which includes each ward's population and boundaries—

(i) after a decennial census, as the Minnesota election law provides;

(ii) when required by law or judicial decree, as the law or decree provides; or

(iii) when the number of wards changes, 60 days after the amendment takes effect (even if the change takes effect later).

(B) Public hearings. The Commission must hold at least four public hearings before adopting a ward-boundary plan, and must hold at least two of those hearings after—

(i) giving public notice of a draft plan or plans for at least seven days before each hearing; and

(ii) inviting comments from each neighborhood organization recognized by the City Council.

If the Commission reestablishes ward boundaries before the legislature has been redistricted, the ward boundaries may be modified after the legislature has been redistricted for the purpose of establishing precinct boundaries. If ward boundaries are modified, the Commission will determine whether any additional hearings will be held to consider the modifications.

(C) Adoption. The Commission adopts a ward-boundary plan by a majority of its membership at a meeting of which it has given public notice. The adopted plan takes effect when the Commission files it with the City Clerk.

(D) Applicability. A ward-boundary plan applies to the first general election for which filing opens after the plan takes effect. A plan does not affect the eligibility or term of any incumbent holding office when the plan takes effect, unless otherwise provided in section 3.2(d).

(4) Funding. The City Council must provide for the staff and other resources that the Commission needs.

(5) Ordinances. The City Council may enact any necessary or prudent ordinance implementing this section 2.2(c). No such ordinance applies to any redistricting process that begins within 30 days.

(6) Jurisdiction. The district court enjoys original jurisdiction over any case arising out of redistricting under this section 2.2(c).

(Ord. No. 2016-086, § 1, 12-9-16, eff. 3-12-17; Ord. No. 2020-057, § 1, 11-3-20, eff. 12-3-20)

children.title: Park districts
children.text:
The provisions of the preceding section 2.2 regarding redistricting wards likewise apply as far as possible to redistricting park districts, except as this section 2.3 or a general or special law otherwise provides.

(a) Number. The City comprises six park districts, designated by number. If possible, a redistricted park district keeps the number of the former district from which its population mostly came.

(b) Commission. For this section 2.3's purposes, the "Commission" means the Charter Commission.

(c) Park and Recreation Board. Before holding the last two public hearings on any park-district boundary plan, the Commission must notify the Park and Recreation Board of a draft plan or plans. The Commission must consider any recommendation by the Board.

If the Commission reestablishes park district boundaries before the legislature has been redistricted, the park district boundaries may be modified after the legislature has been redistricted for the purpose of establishing precinct boundaries. If park district boundaries are modified, the Commission must notify the Park and Recreation Board of a draft plan or plans. The Commission must consider any recommendation by the Board. The Commission will determine whether any additional hearings will be held to consider the modifications.

(Ord. No. 2020-057, § 2, 11-3-20, eff. 12-3-20)

children.title: Precincts
children.text:
(a) Precincts, polling places. For the convenient administration of elections, the City Council must divide each ward into precincts and designate a polling place in each precinct. Each precinct must lie wholly within a single ward and park district.

(b) Effective date. An act dividing a ward into precincts, or designating a polling place, takes effect as the Minnesota election law provides.

(Ord. No. 2016-086, § 2, 12-9-16, eff. 3-12-17)

children.title: Annexed territory
children.text: Any annexed territory joins the ward and the park district to which it is adjacent or, if adjacent to more than one ward or district, the least populous such ward or district.

children.title: Special districts
children.text:
For the more efficient delivery of municipal services in the City and its surroundings, and with a view toward their orderly growth—

(a) the City Council may designate any area within three miles of the City's boundaries as a special district, in which it may—

(1) lay out the streets and other infrastructure so that they consistently continue the City's system;

(2) accept or dedicate property for streets or any other public purpose; and

(3) plat the district accordingly; and

(b) except as prohibited by law, the City may acquire realty and extend infrastructure beyond the City's boundaries without designating a special district.

children.title: General provisions
children.text:
(a) General law applies. Unless it is inconsistent with this charter, the Minnesota election law applies to each municipal election.

(b) Voting method. The voters elect the City's elected officers by single transferable voting (also known as "ranked-choice voting" or "instant-runoff voting"). The City Council must provide by ordinance the method of counting the votes and of breaking a tie.

(c) Administration. The City Clerk administers each election under the City Council's direction. The clerk must give public notice of the time and place of holding each election at least 15 days before the election.

(d) Ballots. The City Council must provide by ordinance for the ballot's format.

(1) Nonpartisan ballot. The ballot for each elected office is a nonpartisan ballot. Each candidate for Mayor or for Council member may state, in up to three words, his or her political party or principle, which will appear on the ballot.

(2) Order. The candidates' names must appear on a single ballot, which lists the offices being elected in this order:

(A) Mayor;

(B) Council member;

(C) Board of Estimate and Taxation member;

(D) Park and Recreation commissioner at large; and

(E) Park and Recreation commissioner by district.

children.title: Regular elections
children.text:
(a) Election years. A regular general election occurs in the last calendar year before any elected officer's term expires.

(b) Regular general election. The City holds its regular general election on the uniform municipal election day for which the Minnesota election law provides.

(c) Schedule. For each regular general election, the City Council must provide by ordinance for a filing period of at least 15 days, unless the law provides otherwise. No act scheduling a filing period applies to any election held in the same calendar year.

(d) Redistricting and Elections. If a Minnesota election law requires any additional City council election, other than a regular general election or a special election required under this charter, and the additional required election is based, in part, on the results of a decennial federal census, the City will hold an election for Council members in compliance with that Minnesota Statute. If an additional required Council member election must be held, the existing term will be for two years. The term for Council members after the additional required election will be the remainder of the four-year term that would have been served by Council members if an election would not have been required under this section 3.2(d).

The individuals who are elected in the additional required election will take office as provided in section 8.2(d), the same as a regular general election.

(Ord. No. 2020-057, § 3, 11-3-20, eff. 12-3-20)

children.title: Special elections
children.text:
(a) Elected office. When a vacancy occurs in an elected office before the term expires, and this charter does not provide another method of filling the vacancy, a special election must be held on a legal election day under Minnesota election law that is more than 90 days from the date of the vacancy. For each special election, the City Council must provide by ordinance for a filing period of at least eight days.

(b) Other special elections. The City Council must schedule a special election as required by law on any question that the voters may lawfully decide, and may schedule any other lawful special election, in accordance with Minnesota election law. This section 3.3(b) is subject to section 9.4(e).

(Ord. No. 2020-058, § 1, 11-3-20, eff. 12-3-20)

children.title: Candidacy
children.text:
(a) Affidavit of candidacy. A candidate's name appears on the ballot if the candidate files an affidavit of candidacy with the City Clerk and either—

(1) Pays to the clerk the filing fee for which section 3.4(b) provides, or

(2) Presents to the clerk a petition in place of the filing fee with the number of signatures for which the Minnesota election law provides.

(b) Filing fee. The filing fee is—

(1) for Mayor, $500.00;

(2) for Council member, $250.00;

(3) for Board of Estimate and Taxation member, $100.00; and

(4) for Park and Recreation Commissioner, $100.00.

(PLC-174, § 1, 11-4-14, eff. 1-2-15)

children.heading: ARTICLE IV.
children.title: CITY COUNCIL
children.text: For this charter's purposes, the "Council" means the City Council for which this article IV provides.

children.title: Function
children.text:
(a) Legislative body. The legislative body is the City Council, in which the City's general legislative, policymaking authority, and oversight resides.

(b) Scope. The Council may act on the City's behalf in any matter, except where—

(1) this charter reserves the action for a different board, commission, or committee, or for the Mayor or the administration for which article VII provides; or

(2) the action is inconsistent with this charter or otherwise unlawful.

(c) Council as statutory board.

(1) Generally. Where the law provides for municipal action through a board or commission, and this charter does not reserve that authority to a board or commission other than the Council, the Council must either—

(A) itself serve as the board or commission for which the law provides, even if the board or commission is a statutory rather than a municipal agency; or

(B) provide by ordinance for the board or commission, in which case—
